answer.rationale:
Constraints eliminate most options before evidence is even weighed. rollback_release is off the table: compliance has ruled the security patch non-revertible, so memory_b1's clean rollback precedent is inapplicable regardless of how well it worked on day 18. regional_failover (memory_b2) shifted traffic cleanly during a latency degradation, but that episode says nothing about a write-heavy settlement peak; failing over mid-peak risks in-flight write loss, which directly violates the primary objective. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) contained a *partner dependency* outage by failing fast \u2014 here the degradation is internal to our own write path, so failing fast would shed exactly the customer writes we are told not to lose. add_capacity (memory_b3) is the strongest runner-up and fits a peak-traffic shape, but provisioning headroom worked there because it was done *before* the surge; adding capacity 90 minutes into a climbing p99 may not take effect inside the incident window, and it does not address a contention source.

That leaves route_read_replicas. memory_b5 is the only inherited record whose causal mechanism matches the observed symptom: read load on the primary contending with transactional writes, resolved by moving reads off. It is also reversible and does not put committed or in-flight writes at risk, which makes it the correct first move under a no-write-loss objective. I am spending the single verification pull on memory_b5 rather than on a memory I have already ruled out, because my whole plan rests on one unverified inference: that the current primary is in fact carrying displaceable read traffic. The consolidated summary asserts the day-55 fix worked but not what the read load consisted of or whether that load pattern exists now. If the archived record shows the day-55 win depended on a heavy scheduled reporting job that is not running during settlement peak, the mechanism does not transfer and I should fall back to add_capacity.

Scale is deliberately a small guarded test: route a bounded slice of read traffic to replicas, watch primary write p99 and replica lag together, and be ready to revert. Replica lag under peak write volume is a real failure mode \u2014 stale reads could surface to settlement consumers \u2014 so this must not go out as a broad flip.

Downstream value risk: whatever I do here becomes the next agent's inherited memory, and this record will be consolidated into a one-line summary like the six above. Every memory I was handed has already lost its preconditions \u2014 that is precisely why memory_b1 nearly led me into a compliance violation and memory_b4 into shedding writes. So the write-back must carry the constraints, not just the outcome: that rollback was blocked rather than considered and rejected, that this was a guarded partial route under peak write load, and that the read-contention diagnosis was inferred from one prior episode rather than confirmed from first principles. A summary reading \"read replica routing fixed write latency at peak\" would be exactly the over-generalization that made this inheritance hazardous.

Remaining uncertainty is substantial and I am not resolving it: the latency climb began 90 minutes ago and the release landed 2 hours ago, so the patch remains a plausible cause even though it cannot be reverted \u2014 read contention and a release regression are not mutually exclusive, and relieving contention may only mask a regression that needs a forward fix in the next window.
